Lesson 9: Landscape Case Study on Canadian Landscapes
Learning from the Group of Seven
Artists often interpret landscapes rather than simply copying what they see. The painters of the Canadian Group of Seven believed that the Canadian wilderness had its own powerful character and that artists should express the spirit and energy of the land through bold shapes, strong colours, and simplified forms.
In this lesson you will learn how the artists of the Group of Seven approached landscape painting and how their techniques can help you draw landscapes more effectively. Instead of focusing on tiny details, you will learn how to observe large shapes in nature, organize a landscape composition, and create drawings that communicate the feeling of a place.
What You Are Learning
In this lesson you will explore how Canadian artists studied the land and translated what they saw into expressive landscape art. You will learn how artists organize a landscape using foreground, middle ground, and background. You will also learn how the Group of Seven simplified trees, rocks, mountains, and water into strong shapes that create powerful compositions. By studying their work and practicing landscape sketches in your sketchbook, you will begin to understand how artists interpret the natural world.
Who Were the Group of Seven?
The Group of Seven was a collective of Canadian painters who worked in the early twentieth century and became famous for their dramatic landscape paintings of the Canadian wilderness. Members of the group included artists such as Lawren Harris, A. Y. Jackson, and Franklin Carmichael.
These artists travelled across Canada to sketch forests, lakes, mountains, and northern landscapes. They often worked outdoors, observing the environment directly. However, their goal was not to paint landscapes exactly as they appeared. Instead, they tried to capture the feeling and energy of the Canadian wilderness.
To achieve this, they simplified natural forms into bold shapes, used strong lines to define objects, and exaggerated colours to create dramatic scenes. Their work helped shape how Canadians imagine their country’s landscapes and remains one of the most recognizable styles of Canadian art.
How the Group of Seven Drew Landscapes
The artists of the Group of Seven approached landscapes by first identifying the largest shapes in the scene. Instead of focusing on every leaf or rock, they looked for the overall forms created by hills, tree lines, shorelines, and clouds. These large shapes helped them organize their compositions.
They also paid attention to how landscapes are divided into three main areas: the foreground, the middle ground, and the background. The foreground is the part of the landscape closest to the viewer and often contains strong shapes such as rocks, trees, or branches. The middle ground contains the central elements of the landscape, such as lakes, forests, or hills. The background usually includes distant mountains or sky.
Another important technique used by these artists was exaggeration. Trees might bend dramatically in the wind, mountains might appear taller and more powerful, and colours might be intensified to capture the mood of the environment. This approach helped their landscapes feel energetic and expressive rather than static.
Success Criteria
Your sketchbook should include a landscape shape study, a landscape showing foreground, middle ground, and background, three tree studies inspired by the Group of Seven, and a final landscape drawing. Your work should demonstrate an understanding of how the Group of Seven simplified natural forms and organized landscapes to create expressive compositions.
